title: Plug a fibre patch cable's SFP end into a slanted network card's left port
instruction: Take the cable's gold SFP plug out of its slanted holder and push it, tip first, all the way into the network card's left SFP port (the one nearer the left arm). The cable's blue SC plug stays in its tray.
context: Patching a fibre cable into a switch or server card is routine data-centre work and still done by hand. The plug fits only tip first, in line with the port, and the card's ports are slanted, so the hand must follow a 45-degree axis while a cable drags on the plug.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), on the station table. Network card: a PCIe card model (green PCB, steel parts), fixed in a steel cradle that leans it back 45 degrees (top edge toward the arms), square to the arms; only its upper part is modelled, 12 cm wide, 2.1 cm thick, fixed. Its top edge carries two steel SFP ports whose openings face up and toward the arms along the 45-degree axis: each 14.0 mm wide, 9.0 mm tall and 48.9 mm deep inside, 23.2 mm apart, the middle between the two mouths at x 30, y 8. Left port: the one at the larger y. Each mouth has a 2 mm flared lead-in made of four thin steel plates at 45 degrees. Cable: a yellow fibre cable, 5 mm thick, 12 g, a chain of 20 mm segments with soft bending joints, friction 1.2. Its SFP plug (gold) is a rigid body 47.3 mm long, 13.75 mm wide and 8.6 mm tall, 20 g, with a 14 x 12.2 mm latch end 11.5 mm long; it lies in a fixed steel holder (plate, two side rails 17 mm apart with lips, end stop under its tip) that leans it back 45 degrees the same way, tip down, origin at x 24, y 30. Its SC plug (blue) is a 26 x 25 x 10 mm, 40 g body lying in a fixed steel tray at x 14, y -10 and held in place, the cable leaving its back end and draping over the table to the SFP plug. Holder, tray and card stand on thin steel base plates. One fixed starting layout.
scoring: Measured on the SFP plug's tip: depth is how far its tip is below the port mouth, along the port's axis. 1.0: tip depth at least 40 mm in the left port, plug within 3 degrees of the port axis, and the plug at rest (under 3 cm/s) at the end of a 1 s hold. 0.5: depth at least 20 mm in the left port, within 10 degrees of the port axis. 0.25: depth at least 5 mm in the left port, same angle as 0.5. Otherwise 0. The tip must also be within 1.5 mm of the port's centre line at the mouth, or 4.5 mm once it is inside. Any other outcome scores 0, including the right port or a plug that falls off the table. Real-world check: at 40 mm depth, at most about 7 mm of the plug body is still outside the port, and a phone level on the plug reads within 3 degrees of the card's 45-degree lean.
reset_notes: Lay the SFP plug back in its holder, tip down against the stop, and the SC plug in its tray; the cable settles in about 1.5 s.
fidelity: Plug and port sizes are the box colliders of the public AIC SFP module and NIC card models (Apache-2.0), unmodified: the port is 14.0 x 9.0 mm inside and the plug body 13.75 x 8.6 mm, so the clearance is about 0.13 mm a side in width, as in the real models. The one addition is a 2 mm flared lead-in at each port mouth, which a real cage also has, to let an open-loop robot land the plug in simulation. The plug stops at about 41.5 mm depth where its latch shoulder meets the port, so full depth is scored at 40 mm. Only the card's upper part is modelled. The cable is a 12 g soft chain of rigid segments, not a real fibre: no twisting stiffness, lighter than a real patch cable, and no latch spring, click, electrical or optical contact, so no insertion force. The plug shapes are boxes, not the detailed meshes.
